scenes.title: CTE Basics
scenes.narration: A common table expression, defined with the WITH clause, gives a query a named temporary result set that you can reference like a table.

scenes.title: Why use a CTE
bullets: It improves readability by naming an intermediate step.
It can be referenced multiple times within the same query.
It replaces deeply nested subqueries with a top down flow.
It is scoped to the single statement that defines it.
scenes.narration: A CTE improves readability because you give a meaningful name to an intermediate result instead of burying it in nested parentheses. Once defined, that name can be referenced multiple times in the same query without repeating the logic. It flattens complex nested subqueries into a clear top down structure. Remember that the CTE exists only for the duration of the statement that defines it.

scenes.title: Anatomy of a WITH clause
steps: Name the CTE and list its columns optionally
Reference the CTE name in the main query
scenes.narration: You open with the WITH keyword and give the CTE a name. Inside AS and parentheses you place the query that produces the result set. From there the main query can reference the CTE by name just as if it were a real table.

scenes.title: A single CTE for high earners
scenes.code:
WITH high_earners AS (
    SELECT employee_id, first_name, salary, dept_id
    FROM employees
    WHERE salary > 100000
)
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS num_high_earners
FROM high_earners
GROUP BY dept_id;
scenes.narration: Here the CTE named high_earners selects everyone paid more than one hundred thousand. The main query then treats high_earners like a table, grouping those rows by department to count how many high earners each one has. This reads far more clearly than embedding the filter inside a subquery.

scenes.title: Multiple CTEs chained together
scenes.code:
WITH dept_avg AS (
    SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
    FROM employees
    GROUP BY dept_id
),
above_avg AS (
    SELECT e.employee_id, e.first_name, e.dept_id
    FROM employees e
    JOIN dept_avg d ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id
    WHERE e.salary > d.avg_salary
)
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS num_above_avg
FROM above_avg
GROUP BY dept_id;
scenes.narration: You can define several CTEs by separating them with commas. The first CTE, dept_avg, computes each department's average salary. The second CTE, above_avg, joins back to it to find employees paid above their department average, and later CTEs may reference earlier ones. The final query then counts those employees per department.

scenes.text: A CTE is not guaranteed to be materialized. Many engines inline it into the main query, so treat it as a readability tool rather than a performance hint.
scenes.narration: Do not assume a CTE is computed once and stored, because many engines simply inline its definition into the surrounding query. Think of CTEs primarily as a way to make complex SQL readable rather than as a performance optimization.
